content: 1. Antiviral therapy coverage among eligible HBsAg-positive pregnant women is a critical metric for monitoring the prevention of mother-to-child transmission of hepatitis B. This is tracked globally through the Global AIDS Monitoring system. 2. The number of needles and syringes distributed per person who injects drugs annually is an essential harm-reduction indicator. It is monitored to reduce the transmission of bloodborne infections, including hepatitis C, among people who inject drugs. 3. The coverage of opioid agonist maintenance therapy among people who inject drugs is another key indicator. This therapy is vital for reducing the risk of hepatitis C transmission and improving health outcomes in this population. 4. The proportion of healthcare facilities that administer safe injections is a critical measure of blood and injection safety. This is assessed through health facility surveys to ensure compliance with safety standards. 5. The proportion of blood units screened for bloodborne diseases is a global indicator of blood safety. This ensures that transfusions are free from infections such as hepatitis B and C. 6. The proportion of people with chronic hepatitis B who have been diagnosed is a key metric for understanding the diagnostic gap and improving access to care. 7. Similarly, the proportion of people with chronic hepatitis C who have been diagnosed highlights the need for enhanced diagnostic efforts to link individuals to curative treatments. 8. The proportion of people diagnosed with chronic hepatitis B who initiate treatment is a critical measure of linkage to care and treatment initiation. 9. The proportion of people with chronic hepatitis B currently receiving treatment reflects the ongoing management of the disease and the effectiveness of treatment programs. 10. The proportion of people diagnosed with chronic hepatitis C who initiate treatment is a key indicator of access to curative therapies. 11. The proportion of people with chronic hepatitis B who receive annual follow-up, particularly those not initiating treatment, is an important measure of disease monitoring and management. 12. The proportion of treatment attrition among people with chronic hepatitis B within a reporting year is a critical indicator of retention in care and treatment adherence. 13. The proportion of people with chronic hepatitis C who are treated and achieve a cure is a measure of the success of curative therapies and program effectiveness. 14. The proportion of people with chronic hepatitis B who are treated and achieve HBV DNA viral suppression is a key outcome indicator for treatment efficacy. 15. The incidence of hepatitis B, measured as HBsAg prevalence among children aged five years and younger, is a critical impact indicator for monitoring the success of prevention programs, including vaccination. 16. The incidence of hepatitis C is another global impact indicator, reflecting the effectiveness of prevention and treatment strategies. 17. The mother-to-child transmission rate of HBV is a key additional indicator for assessing the success of interventions aimed at preventing perinatal transmission. 18. Deaths attributable to hepatocellular carcinoma, cirrhosis, and chronic liver diseases caused by chronic hepatitis B and C are critical impact indicators for understanding the mortality burden of these infections. 19. Core indicators are those deemed feasible to collect, monitor, and track in most contexts, while additional indicators are desirable but may not be feasible in all settings. Global indicators are a subset of core indicators highly relevant for global monitoring and reporting to the World Health Assembly. 20. Approximately 20–30% of people with hepatitis B may develop progressive liver disease or hepatocellular carcinoma and are eligible for treatment with nucleoside analogue therapies. 21. Consolidated guidelines on person-centered viral hepatitis strategic information emphasize the use of data to support the scale-up of hepatitis prevention, diagnosis, and treatment services at the country level. 22. Hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infections are major global health concerns due to their high prevalence and associated mortality. Together, they account for a significant burden of disease and increasing deaths from cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. 23. In 2022, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimated that 254 million people were living with chronic HBV and 50 million with chronic HCV worldwide. Annually, 2 million new HBV and HCV infections occur. 24. The burden of chronic HBV and HCV infections is geographically and demographically concentrated, with two-thirds of the global burden in the 10 most severely affected countries. 25. In the WHO African and Western Pacific Regions, approximately 5% of the general population lives with chronic HBV infection. However, only 13% of people with chronic HBV infection had been diagnosed, and close to 3% had received antiviral therapy by the end of 2022. 26. Between 2015 and 2022, only 36% of people with chronic HCV had been diagnosed, and 20% had received curative treatment, highlighting the need for better linkage between diagnosis and care. 27. Sharing of injection equipment among people who inject drugs is a major contributor to the global HCV epidemic, accounting for an estimated 44% of new HCV infections in 2022. 28. Other affected populations include healthcare workers, people in prisons or closed settings, and individuals receiving frequent blood transfusions, such as those with hemophilia, thalassemia, or undergoing dialysis. 29. Significant progress has been made in eliminating perinatal transmission of HBV through universal infant HBV immunization, including timely hepatitis B birth doses. However, global birth-dose coverage was only 45% in 2022, with the lowest coverage (18%) in the WHO African Region. 30. In May 2016, the World Health Assembly endorsed the global health sector strategy on viral hepatitis 2016–2021, aiming to eliminate viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030. 31. To achieve elimination, the strategy focuses on five core interventions: HBV vaccination for infants, prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HBV, blood and injection safety, harm-reduction services for people who inject drugs, and testing and treatment coverage. 32. WHO recommends lifelong treatment for eligible individuals with hepatitis B and short-course curative treatment for hepatitis C. 33. The new strategy for 2022–2030 integrates efforts across HIV, hepatitis, and sexually transmitted infections, with five strategic directions: delivering high-quality, evidence-based, people-centered services; optimizing systems and partnerships; using data to drive decisions; engaging communities; and fostering innovation. 34. Member states are encouraged to strengthen information systems for viral hepatitis and integrate them into broader health information systems to enable data triangulation for analysis. 35. Strengthening surveillance and monitoring of advanced liver diseases and hepatocellular carcinoma is essential for analyzing mortality attributable to viral hepatitis. 36. The guidelines emphasize person-centered monitoring, prioritizing indicators that support prevention, diagnosis, and treatment interventions, and recommend stepwise guidance for building robust health information systems. 37. The updated guidelines include a strategic information framework with 10 core global indicators, a menu of additional indicators, and a cascade of care indicators for viral hepatitis. 38. A new section on person-centered data monitoring supports the delivery of prevention, diagnosis, and treatment interventions, including a minimum data set and updated patient management templates. 39. The guidelines provide stepwise recommendations for implementing country surveillance systems at different levels of maturity to improve programs and address gaps. 40. Consolidated metadata offer detailed information on hepatitis-related indicator definitions and measurement methods.
